posts.title: How I Learned To Write for a General Audience
posts.reason: Directly states that he learned to write for general audiences by stripping out jargon and explaining why his technical work matters, which is the core of the question.

posts.title: Trade Books and Scholarly Books
posts.reason: Explains that Misquoting Jesus was a trade-book version of his broader textual-criticism scholarship and that he made it digestible for normal readers.

posts.title: Writing Scholarly and Popular Books on the Same Topic
posts.reason: Directly explains that he turns scholarly work into a trade book by making it “digestible for normal human beings,” and says Misquoting Jesus popularized his textual-criticism scholarship for untrained readers.

posts.title: Communicating with Non-Scholars
posts.reason: Directly explains that writing for non-scholars requires removing jargon and making complicated scholarship accessible without dumbing it down, and ties that skill to his first trade book.

posts.title: Balancing the Scholarly and the Popular
posts.reason: Discusses the challenge of maintaining both scholarly and popular writing and stresses adapting to a nonexpert audience, but it is more about balancing careers than the conversion process itself.

posts.title: Scholars and Popular Audiences
posts.reason: The post directly explains Bart’s approach to popular books: he says scholars must translate technical scholarship for ‘your mother and the guy across the street,’ choose a nonspecialist audience, and communicate simply without oversimplifying or condescending.

posts.title: Trying to Make Scholarship Interesting
posts.reason: Gives a concrete account of learning to make technical material interesting and understandable for lay readers, then applying that skill to textbooks and trade books.

posts.title: Who Should Write Trade Books?
posts.reason: Mostly argues that trade books should be written by experts and warns against non-expert books; it only indirectly touches on communicating scholarship to the general public.

questions.question: How did early Christians understand wealth, almsgiving, and responsibility toward the poor?

posts.title: What the Earliest *Christians* Thought About Wealth
posts.reason: Explains early Christian attitudes toward wealth and the poor, contrasting euergetism with almsgiving and emphasizing giving to beggars and the needy.

posts.title: You Mean Everyone (Except the Truly Destitute) Needs to Give? But How Much?
posts.reason: Directly answers the question by describing early Christian expectations that everyone give, the redemptive value of almsgiving, and the rich-poor relationship in salvation.

posts.title: Softening Jesus’ Message on Giving up (Literally) Everything
posts.reason: Directly explains early Christian views of wealth, almsgiving, and the duty to support the poor, citing Paul’s collection, Hermas, and the shift from divestment to generosity.

posts.title: Did Christians Invent Charity?
posts.reason: Strongly relevant because it outlines the Christian shift toward caring for the poor and contrasts it with Greco-Roman views of wealth and giving.

posts.title: “Redemptive Gifts”: Can Giving to Charity Save Your Soul?
posts.reason: Closely addresses how early Christians thought charity could aid salvation and how wealthy believers were expected to give to the poor, with examples from the Didache, Polycarp, and Chrysostom.

posts.title: Were Early Christians Really Charitable?  Or Was It All Talk?
posts.reason: Directly discusses early Christian charitable practice and responsibility toward the poor, including church collections, widows and orphans, and institutional support.

posts.title: Love in Action: Christian Views of Charitable Giving
posts.reason: Directly discusses early Christian charitable giving, wealth, and responsibility toward the needy, including the move from self-giving to almsgiving.

posts.title: The New Book I’m Writing About Altruism:  Putting It In a Nutshell
posts.reason: Relevant background on Christianity’s moral obligation to help strangers and the poor, but it is mainly about altruism and modern conscience rather than early Christian wealth or almsgiving in detail.

posts.title: How I Begin My Book on Jesus, Ethics, and Altruism
posts.reason: The post directly discusses Jesus and early Christianity as grounding an obligation to care for the poor and needy, including almsgiving and charity, but it gives only broad thesis-level treatment and little specific detail about wealth.

posts.title: Love.  How I’ve Shifted the Focus of My Book on Charity.
posts.reason: Meaningfully addresses the Christian ethic of love as helping those in need and connects it to charitable giving, though the post is broader than the specific wealth-and-poor question.

posts.title: The Good Done By Christianity to Our World
posts.reason: Only indirectly relevant: it broadly praises Christian concern for others and later institutions for the poor, but does not really analyze early Christian ideas about wealth or almsgiving.
